analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the federal agency that investigates toxic chemical exposures in communities.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has had no further action since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, the federal health agency that investigates and responds to communities' exposure to hazardous substances — for example, people living near Superfund waste sites, chemical plants, or contaminated water supplies. It would move the national disease and toxic-exposure registries to some other part of the Department of Health and Human Services, but every other function of the agency would end within a year. The bill has no cosponsors and has not moved since it was referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that generate hazardous waste or discharge toxic substances benefit if the bill passes. The agency being abolished performs public health assessments at contaminated sites, documents which chemicals sickened nearby residents, and provides the health data that communities use when seeking site cleanups and accountability. Removing that investigator would reduce one source of scrutiny of toxic exposure. No other members of Congress have joined the bill, so support is currently limited to its sponsor.

how_it_helps.text: The bill abolishes the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, effective one year after enactment, terminating all of its functions except those explicitly transferred.

Only two narrow duties would survive: the Secretary of Health and Human Services would move the national registry of serious diseases and the registry of persons exposed to toxic substances to some other HHS agency, at the Secretary's discretion.

The bill strikes the agency's role from more than a dozen environmental and health laws, including the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act's Great Lakes provisions, the Solid Waste Disposal Act, and Toxic Substances Control Act consultation requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Residents of communities near hazardous waste sites, contaminated military installations, and industrial pollution would bear the cost. They would lose the federal agency that investigates whether their health problems are linked to chemical exposures and that responds when communities ask for help. Removing the agency's consultations from water, air, and waste laws would also leave those programs without the environmental-health expertise the law currently requires.

drawbacks.text: Communities exposed to toxic substances would lose the dedicated federal agency that investigates their exposures and publishes health assessments; the bill transfers only the disease and exposure registries, terminating every other ATSDR function.

The destination for the surviving registries is left to the HHS Secretary's discretion ('an appropriate agency'), so the databases tracking who was exposed to what would lose their dedicated staff and structure, and the bill directs transfers of personnel, funds, and records only for those registries, not for the agency's field investigations.

The bill strikes the agency's required consultations from water, air, waste, and defense laws — for example, dropping ATSDR from Great Lakes water-quality consultations and deleting Solid Waste Disposal Act provisions on the agency — leaving those programs with no environmental-health partner in the process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers no replacement for the agency's core work. It saves whatever a small standalone agency costs and tidies the law books, but communities facing chemical contamination would lose the federal health investigator that tells them what they were exposed to and what it might be doing to them. The registries would survive on paper, but the field investigations, exposure assessments, and health consultations that actually help affected neighborhoods would end.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 3, 2025, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and has not moved since — no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 3, 2025, the first day of the 119th Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; the action history shows no further steps since.
No other House member has cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position — the bill simply has not advanced. Communities near contaminated sites have lost nothing yet, and the polluting interests the bill would relieve have gained nothing either; the main beneficiary of the status quo is the public, which still has the agency investigating toxic exposures.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, for now — the bill went nowhere

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral in January 2025 — no markup, hearing, or floor schedule.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the sponsor's own party colleagues gave the bill no cosponsors, so no party-level support or opposition is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and other toxic-substance emitters
industries.note: ATSDR evaluates health risks at hazardous waste sites and documents community exposures, which feeds into cleanup pressure and public accountability. Abolishing it would remove a federal health investigator whose findings often cut against facilities that generate hazardous waste.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste generators and landfill operators
industries.note: The bill deletes ATSDR's role from Solid Waste Disposal Act provisions and other waste-related statutes, reducing the environmental-health scrutiny tied to waste sites.

industries.industry: Environmental consulting and public-health assessment field
industries.note: The bill terminates a federal employer and programmatic customer in the exposure-assessment field, a minor workforce effect alongside the main public-health stakes.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action in the first months of the Congress, the bill will almost certainly die quietly in committee at the end of this Congress, as most referred bills do; it could be reintroduced in a future Congress.
